title: Majority outside constant-depth modular circuits
formal: Is \(\mathrm{MAJ}\notin\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\)? Precisely, for every fixed modulus \(m\geq2\), depth bound \(d\geq1\), constants \(C\geq1\), \(k\geq1\), and \(N\geq1\), is there an input length \(n\geq N\) for which no depth-at-most-\(d\) circuit over AND, OR, NOT and \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\), with at most \(C(n+1)^k\) gates, computes \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}\) exactly?
why: Majority is a basic threshold operation. Showing that constant-depth modular circuits cannot compute it would separate ordinary threshold counting from the full fixed-modulus ACC⁰ model on a simple explicit function.
status_note: The target is explicitly open in Jukna’s source. A 13 September 2026 small-text check of later modular-circuit work identified a symmetry-restricted AND result, not a solution for majority in unrestricted ACC⁰. No resolution was verified; status remains source_open.

progress.text: Research Problem 12.28 explicitly poses Majority outside ACC⁰ after discussing known lower bounds for more complex languages.

The preprint Optimal Lower Bounds for Symmetric Modular Circuits treats AND and syntactically symmetric modular circuits. Its abstract was checked for possible overlap and does not settle unrestricted majority in ACC⁰.

sentences: Majority returns one when at least half of its input bits are one.
ACC⁰ circuits combine Boolean operations and modular-counting gates using constant depth and polynomial size.
The question asks whether every fixed choice of modulus and depth fails to compute majority within polynomial size.
Known results for prime moduli or additional circuit restrictions do not settle the full composite-modulus question.
A separation would show that this shallow modular model cannot express a basic threshold operation efficiently.

definitions: For \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}(x)=1\) if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\geq\lceil n/2\rceil\). An ACC circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with one output, unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and constants. A \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\) gate outputs one precisely when the sum of its Boolean inputs is divisible by \(m\). Depth is the maximum number of noninput gates on an input-output path, including NOT gates. Size is the number of noninput gates; counting wires instead gives the same polynomial-size class. The modulus, depth and polynomial-size constants are fixed for the whole family and cannot depend on \(n\). Circuits may be chosen separately for every length, without any construction algorithm, uniformity or bound on fan-out. The class \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\) is the union of these polynomial-size, constant-depth families over all fixed moduli. Allowing a fixed finite collection of moduli is equivalent, by using their common multiple with a constant-size gate substitution. All assignments must be computed correctly; no probability of error is allowed.

context_blocks.text: Jukna’s Research Problem 12.28 asks whether Majority lies outside ACC⁰. This is a lower bound for one concrete counting function, stronger in explicitness than separating a large uniform complexity class from the circuit class.

Prime-modulus lower bounds and the separation of nondeterministic exponential time from ACC⁰ concern different targets from the full majority question. In particular, results for prime moduli do not cover arbitrary composite moduli such as six.

Pago’s 2026 work proves lower bounds for computing AND using modular gates under syntactic symmetry assumptions. The permitted gate basis, target function and symmetry restriction differ from the unrestricted majority circuits in this card, so that result does not resolve this question.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal lower-bound statement, or refute it by proving the existence of fixed \(m,d,C,k\) and circuits of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\) computing majority for every input length. Refuting one fixed size exponent is insufficient for a positive answer. Results for a prime modulus, a restricted wiring symmetry, uniform circuits alone or a different hard function do not meet the complete criterion.
